result.graft: From B: add one default-off, provider-named Model consent switch on the Connect sheet that enables Connect, making permission active and explicit without restoring a second sheet.
result.defense: C best serves the fewest-taps goal while covering the acceptance list: one provider-named consent at Connect with Privacy details, per-provider field, Message Chief after connect, inline failed-key recovery, no-model Not sent with Connect, an actionable empty thread, hidden + until connected, and the consequence/confirm when turning Model off. A fixes labels and adds states with least effort, but keeping the first-send sheet violates the one-consent-moment rule and interrupts the user at the exact moment of the first reply. B gives one Continue action, yet its upfront Model/Speech/Memory switches demand uninformed decisions about unused features, conflate separate data flows, omit the stated Privacy link, per-provider field and missing-state drawings, and carries the highest restructuring risk. C's only weakness is footer-implied consent, which the single grafted B switch resolves without adding a gate.

Option C is the clear winner because it treats connecting a model as the explicit consent moment, eliminating the redundant second prompt on first send while satisfying every acceptance criterion and screen-state requirement. By placing a concise, provider-specific consent statement and Privacy details link directly beneath the Connect CTA, C gets the founder to their first reply from Chief in the fewest taps without sacrificing informed permission. Option A fails the core goal and acceptance criteria by keeping both gates—interrupting the user's first message to Chief with a second sheet right after they already intentionally configured and connected the provider—and omits the consequence of turning Model off. Option B removes the second prompt but replaces it with a heavy full-screen setup wizard that crowds the compact 466x678 display with premature toggles for Speech and Memory (which are better handled just-in-time on first use, as in C), introduces a contradictory state where a user could connect a model with the Model switch turned off, and leaves the required no-model Home, after-connect card, and not-sent recovery states unaddressed.
